keySentence: Neverland was perfect, but Wendy knew something Peter never did — home matters.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: The night before Wendy left Neverland she sat with Peter for a long and quiet time under the stars. She tried to explain to him what it was that she was going back to London to find and hold onto. It was not just her bedroom or her mother's face or even the smell of familiar things in the morning. It was the particular feeling of being completely known by people who had always been there for her. Peter listened with his head tilted to one side but his eyes were already looking toward the next horizon. He would never quite understand what she meant and that was perhaps the saddest thing about him of all. Neverland was perfect, but Wendy knew something Peter never did — home matters.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Wendy tried one last time to help Peter understand why she was choosing to leave such a remarkable place behind. She told him that home was not simply a location or a building or a collection of comfortable familiar things. It was the experience of being seen clearly by people who had known you long enough to understand you completely. In Neverland everyone admired Wendy and needed Wendy but nobody had known her since before she could speak. Her mother knew the sound of her footstep on the stair and her father knew which stories made her laugh every time. That kind of knowledge, Wendy said, was something that could only be built slowly over years and years and years. Peter nodded as if he understood, but she could see from his expression that he genuinely and truly did not. Neverland was perfect, but Wendy knew something Peter never did — home matters.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Wendy's departure from Neverland is the moment that separates her story most clearly and permanently from Peter's. Peter will return to Neverland and continue his endless succession of adventures without accumulating wisdom from them. Wendy will return to London, grow up, have children, and eventually become the kind of person her adventures prepared her to be. She takes Neverland with her as a memory and a quality of imagination — but she does not mistake it for a destination. Home, Wendy understands, is not the opposite of adventure but the place that gives adventure its meaning and direction. Without somewhere to return to, adventure is just motion — exciting perhaps, but ultimately pointing nowhere in particular. Peter's tragedy is that he has chosen the motion and given up the meaning, and cannot see what he has lost by doing so. Wendy's gift is that she has understood both things clearly enough to choose between them with her eyes fully open. Neverland was perfect, but Wendy knew something Peter never did — home matters.
